title: The Backup-Heat Boundary: A Two-Person Carbon-Monoxide Check Before the Next Outage
subtitle: A short household walkthrough can clarify which alarms need attention, which backup-heat habits are unsafe, and what everyone should do if an alarm sounds.
imageAlt: Two adults check a carbon-monoxide alarm and its manufacturer label in a hallway near bedroom doors, while a closed notebook rests on a nearby shelf.
imageConcept: A calm, practical scene in a lived-in home: two partners stand together in a hallway, one reading the carbon-monoxide alarm’s manufacturer label while the other records its replacement information in a notebook. Bedroom doors are visible; through a distant window, a generator sits outside, well away from the house.
body: Why make this a two-person check?

A power outage can turn an ordinary question—how will we stay warm or cook?—into a hazardous decision made under pressure. Carbon monoxide (CO) is colorless and odorless, so people cannot rely on sight or smell to detect it. The CDC warns that people who are asleep may die before noticing symptoms. That makes advance planning especially useful: it moves decisions about alarms, equipment and getting outside out of the middle of a cold, stressful night [1].

This is not a test of how prepared a household is, and it does not require one person to act as the safety expert. Two people can walk through the home, compare what they find with alarm instructions and local requirements, then agree on a response. If you live alone, you can still use the same checklist with a trusted friend, neighbor or family member.
Start with the alarms—and their instructions

Walk through the home together and locate every CO alarm. The U.S. Fire Administration recommends alarms outside each separate sleeping area and on every level of the home [2]. Check the manufacturer’s instructions and any applicable local requirements; they govern details such as installation, power source and placement. A battery-operated alarm or one with battery backup can provide protection when electricity is out, as the CDC advises [1].

For each device, write down its location, power source, model if available, and the replacement date specified by its manufacturer. Do not assume an alarm is current because its test button makes a sound: testing and replacement address different things, and the product instructions explain what each signal means. If the date is missing or unclear, find the manual or contact the manufacturer rather than guessing. Make a note of alarms that need batteries, replacement or follow-up, and decide who will handle each task and by when.
Draw a firm line around fuel-burning equipment

During an outage, never use a generator, grill or camp stove inside a home, basement or garage. Do not use a generator outdoors near the building: CDC guidance says to place it outdoors more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents [1]. Keep exhaust directed away from the home, and follow the generator’s own instructions and local guidance. An open garage door does not make a generator in the garage safe; the equipment itself still needs to be outdoors.

Never use a charcoal grill or camp stove inside the home, basement, or garage [3]. A working CO alarm does not make prohibited indoor use safe. Write down the boundary in plain language so nobody has to interpret it while tired: “Generator outside, more than 20 feet from openings; no grill or camp stove inside.” The USFA also advises keeping appliance vents clear of snow and debris [2]. After snow or strong winds, check that vents are unobstructed, following appliance instructions.
Decide what “warm enough” means before the outage

The safest backup plan starts with the heating system and the people who depend on warmth, not with improvising around a fuel-burning appliance. Identify which rooms can be used safely if power fails, how household members will add layers, and where people can go if the home becomes too cold. If anyone has a health condition, mobility limitation, medication concern or other need that changes the plan, include their preferences and consult their clinician or local emergency-management guidance as appropriate.

Fuel-burning heating systems and appliances need proper maintenance. CDC’s cold-weather safety guidance recommends annual service by a qualified technician for fuel-burning heating systems and appliances [3]. That does not replace the manufacturer’s maintenance schedule or a repair when something seems wrong. Put the next service date or unresolved concern on the household list, and agree who will arrange it. If you are unsure whether an appliance can be used during an outage, check its instructions or ask a qualified professional; do not treat an alarm as permission to experiment.
Agree on the response to an alarm

If a CO alarm sounds, everyone should leave the home immediately and call 911 [3]. Choose a meeting place outside and a person who can help anyone who may need assistance leaving. Include children, older adults, guests and pets in the plan, while following emergency responders’ directions about pets and re-entry.

An alarm is not the only reason to act. Symptoms of CO poisoning can include headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion [1]. If someone feels ill and CO exposure is possible, get everyone outside and seek emergency help. Do not spend time troubleshooting the appliance or trying to identify a source indoors. The point of planning is not to diagnose the situation at home; it is to make leaving and contacting emergency services the clear next move.
Make the plan usable in the dark

Keep the written plan somewhere household members can find it, and make a phone photo if that is useful. Include the outside meeting place, emergency number, any household member who may need help exiting, and the person responsible for checking on neighbors or relatives if that is part of the plan. Keep a flashlight accessible without relying on a phone battery, and note where the alarm instructions are stored. These are practical choices, not a substitute for local emergency guidance or device directions.

Then rehearse the shortest version aloud: “Alarm sounds: we go outside, meet at this spot, call 911, and wait for responders before going back in.” If people sleep on different floors or use separate exits, walk the route they would actually take. Make sure nobody is assigned a task that could delay getting out, such as searching for a manual, shutting down a generator or collecting belongings. The USFA’s advice on alarm coverage and clear appliance vents can be checked during the same walk-through [2].
A small review beats a perfect checklist

This conversation may uncover a missing alarm, an unclear replacement date or a heating question that needs a professional. That is useful information, not a reason to rush through purchases or rely on an unverified product claim. Check alarm instructions and applicable local requirements; if an alarm is missing, damaged or beyond its manufacturer’s replacement date, make a specific plan to address it. CDC guidance also stresses following manufacturer replacement instructions [1].

Keep the list modest: what needs attention, who will do it, and when you will check that it is done. If the outage plan changes—because someone moves in, a room becomes a sleeping area, or equipment changes—update the relevant part. A quick review before a forecast outage can help, but the arrangements are more useful when the household has already agreed on them in ordinary conditions.
Close the loop before the forecast turns

Choose one quiet moment this week to do the check together, not during an outage. Start at the sleeping areas and move level by level: locate the alarms, read their labels and instructions, and record any replacement or battery task. Then step outside to identify where a generator could be operated more than 20 feet from doors, windows and vents, or confirm that your household will not use one. Finish by saying the alarm response aloud and pointing out the outdoor meeting place.

Before you put the notes away, give each open task an owner and a date. If you find a concern about an appliance, make the next step a call to a qualified technician or the relevant local authority—not a trial run. The goal is not to predict every complication. It is to make the safest available choice easier to recognize when the house is dark and everyone is tired.
